# Merit-based civil service (examinations) (`merit_civil_service`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/institutions.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Institutions, law & governance (`institutions`)
- Deps: helped by paper, woodblock_printing, universal_schooling
- Core idea: Officials are recruited by open written examination, promoted on record, paid a fixed salary, moved between posts, and barred from serving in their home district. This breaks the hold of hereditary nobles and office-buyers and gives the ruler servants who owe their place to competence. To make the examination fair, cover the candidates' names, have clerks recopy the papers so handwriting cannot be recognised, use several examiners, and search candidates at the gate. Test what the work needs: law, accounts, drafting, practical problems.
- Pitfalls:
  - Examining literary polish instead of useful knowledge: China's eight-legged essay selected for memory and style for centuries
  - 'Open to all' is not equal: preparation took years of leisure, so most graduates came from families that could afford it
  - Low salaries turn examined officials into bribe-takers
  - Where offices are sold (France, the papal court), each office is someone's purchased property and a source of crown revenue: abolishing sale means buying the holders out
  - Telling nobles that birth should not count is an attack on their livelihood and honour
- History: china: 165 BC – Emperor Wen sets written policy questions to recommended candidates; 124 BC Imperial Academy trains officials; c. 600 Sui introduce degrees by written examination; under the Song (960–1279) examinations expand alongside family privilege; names are concealed, and from 1015 palace and metropolitan scripts are recopied to disguise handwriting; abolished 1905; east_asia: 958 – Goryeo Korea adopts the examinations (gwageo); 1075 Vietnam; Japan tried them briefly in the 8th c. and reverted to heredity; india: c. 3rd c. BC–3rd c. AD – Arthashastra advises testing candidates' integrity by secret trials; 1853–1855 open competition for the Indian Civil Service; islamic: 15th–16th c. – Ottoman palace school trains recruited boys (devshirme) and promotes by ability, a merit system within a slave household rather than open examination; europe: 18th c. – Prussia develops qualifying examinations for higher state service; 1854 Northcote–Trevelyan Report proposes open competition in Britain (general from 1870); americas: 1883 – Pendleton Act in the United States
- Read:
  - Benjamin A. Elman, A Cultural History of Civil Examinations in Late Imperial China (2000)
  - John W. Chaffee, The Thorny Gates of Learning in Sung China (1985)
  - Stafford Northcote & Charles Trevelyan, Report on the Organisation of the Permanent Civil Service (1854)
